opus-5.5.text:
I think 2025 felt like the year the field changed gears. In 2023 and 2024 the main story was scaling pretraining: bigger models, more data, more compute, and everyone racing to catch up with the frontier. In 2025 the center of gravity moved to post-training, and especially to reinforcement learning on reasoning. Once people saw that letting a model think longer, explore, and get feedback from verifiable rewards could unlock much stronger math, coding, and problem-solving, the question stopped being only "how big is your model" and became "how well can your model learn from its own attempts."

The second big shift was the open-source community, especially in China. Strong open models and openly shared technical reports showed that a relatively small, focused team could reach near-frontier capability with a fraction of the resources people assumed you needed. That changed the mood. A lot of people inside and outside the industry stopped believing the gap was permanent, and that confidence matters a lot for talent and for what teams are willing to try.

The third thing is that agents became real. In earlier years "agent" was mostly a demo word. This year, coding agents and models that can use tools, browse, and carry out multi-step tasks started doing work people actually rely on. That forces you to think about the model differently. It isn't only answering a question; it's acting in an environment over a long horizon, and the bottlenecks become things like long-context reliability, planning, recovering from mistakes, and efficiency.

So if I had to sum it up: 2025 was when we moved from "models that know a lot" toward "models that can think and act." It was also a humbling year, because every time we solved one problem, the next bottleneck showed up right away. I think that's a sign we're still very early.

r001.rationale: The response describes stronger reasoning through reinforcement learning, longer thinking, and feedback, but it does not identify pushing reasoning to its limits within the chat paradigm as a possible direction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Looking back, I'd describe 2025 as the year AI moved from "impressive demo" to "actually load-bearing." A few things stood out to me.

First, reasoning models matured. The shift toward letting models think longer at inference time, which started showing real results in late 2024, became the default paradigm in 2025. We went from models that could answer questions to models that could work through problems: math, code, multi-step planning. And the cost of that reasoning dropped dramatically over the year. What was expensive and slow in January was cheap and fast by the end of the year.

Second, the open-source story in China changed the global conversation. DeepSeek's releases early in the year showed that frontier-adjacent capability didn't require the compute budgets people assumed. That had ripple effects everywhere: on pricing, on how labs thought about efficiency, on how investors thought about moats. I think it forced everyone to be more honest about what actually drives capability.

Third, and this is the one I find most interesting, agents went from a buzzword to a real product category. Coding agents in particular. Developers started trusting models to take actions, run tools, iterate on their own output, not just suggest a snippet. That's a qualitatively different relationship with the technology. The model is no longer a reference tool; it's a collaborator doing part of the work.

I'd also be honest about what didn't happen. Benchmarks saturated faster than our ability to measure what matters. A lot of agent products were still fragile in practice. And the gap between what models could do in a lab and what organizations could actually deploy reliably stayed wide.

So if 2023 was the year of surprise and 2024 the year of scaling, I'd call 2025 the year of reasoning and agency. The models learned to think and to act. Whether we learn to use that well is more of a 2026 question.

r001.rationale: The response identifies longer inference-time reasoning as a major 2025 development, but it does not specify pushing reasoning within the chat paradigm.

astra-6.text:
I think 2025 is a year of moving from impressive capabilities to figuring out how to make those capabilities genuinely useful. We’ve seen how compelling an AI conversation can be. The harder question is whether a model can handle a complicated task reliably, recognize when it has made a mistake, and work within the resources people actually have.

From a technical perspective, I would pay attention to reasoning and efficiency together. A stronger model matters, but so does how much computation it needs to produce a useful answer. If progress makes these systems more accessible, more people can experiment, and that can lead to applications researchers wouldn’t have anticipated.

So I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t judge the year only by benchmark scores. I’d ask: What can people now accomplish that they couldn’t before? And how much supervision does the model still need? That gap between capability and dependable use is where a lot of the important work lies.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reasoning and compelling AI conversations, but does not identify pushing reasoning to its limits within the chat paradigm as a possible 2025 direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I see 2025 as a year when the focus of AI development shifts from what models can say to what they can actually do. Better reasoning is part of that, but so is the ability to use tools, handle longer tasks, and produce results people can trust.

What interests me most is the relationship between capability and efficiency. A model becoming more powerful matters, but making that capability accessible at a lower cost can have an equally large impact. It allows more researchers and developers to experiment, and that broadens the range of ideas we can explore.

At the same time, I think we need to be careful about equating impressive demonstrations with reliable intelligence. There is still a gap between solving a well-defined problem and working consistently in an open-ended environment. For me, 2025 is about pushing that boundary—and understanding more clearly where the limitations are.

r001.rationale: The response mentions better reasoning and pushing a boundary, but does not identify pushing reasoning to its limits within the chat paradigm as a 2025 direction.
